structured_output.summary:
The most useful new evidence comes from two CIFAR-10 records that beat airbench94_muon (2.59 s): Hiverge at 1.978 s and Fable/Fulcrum at 1.828 s. Both run on an A100-SXM with PyTorch 2.4.0, the same stack as ours.

1. **Progressive resizing works on the airbench lineage (H2.3).** Fable trained 3 epochs at 24 px, 3 at 28 px, then 3 at 32 px, giving about a 10% time cut. Two details matter: lower-resolution images were made by bilinear downsampling of the whole image, not cropping, and the whole run was captured as a CUDA graph. With cropping, or with plain torch.compile, the net gain disappeared.
2. **A big launch-overhead lever that compile flags can't reach (H3/H2).** Per-step overhead was 0.2 ms with the whole run captured as one CUDA graph, versus 1.5–4 ms with plain compile. The optimizer step was also fused into the graph with torch._foreach ops.
3. **Tuned Muon recipe from Hiverge to transplant.** Batch 1536 (not 2000), lr 0.205, momentum 0.655, tuned 3-step Newton-Schulz coefficients, all Newton-Schulz updates batched into one call, SiLU instead of GELU, whitening bias trained for 0.2 epochs instead of 3, a light brightness/contrast jitter, and a shorter 7.65-epoch schedule. Fable also stopped the LR decay at 5% of the peak rather than 0.
4. **Weak or negative evidence for loss-based data filtering (H1.6).** The airbench96_faster filter needs a separate proxy training run and is only shown at the long 96% regime. That proxy run would be timed here.
5. **Turbo-Muon** reports about 3% time savings by dropping one Newton-Schulz iteration, but our recipe already uses only 3.
6. **The earlier source for H1.1 is unreliable.** The PR claiming 75.29% at 8.5 epochs now returns 404. It conflicts with E001 (73.83% with the same settings) and with E007 (Muon beat SGD), so it probably used test-time augmentation.
7. **No public CIFAR-100 submissions exist.** The competition repo has no pull requests, only the ResNet9 baseline (75.36% in 59.3 s).

findings.claim: Fable's CIFAR-10 94% record (1.828 s vs Hiverge 1.978 s, 200 trials each, A100) gets most of its gain from a per-epoch resolution schedule: res_schedule = [24,24,24,28,28,28,32,32,32] over 8.875 epochs. The 28->32 stage saved 0.128 s and adding the 24 px stage saved another 0.081 s. Lower resolution comes from F.interpolate(x, size=res, mode='bilinear', align_corners=False) on the whole augmented image, with the whitening conv unchanged. The final MaxPool2d(3) was replaced by a global max pool so the small maps work. Batch size stays fixed at 1536. LR decays linearly over 8.5 epochs to a floor of 0.05x the peak, not 0.
findings.relevance: Direct evidence for H2.3/H2.3.1 on the same architecture family, GPU and PyTorch version. It suggests H2.3.1 should use whole-image downsampling, not 24 px crops, and a 3-stage 24/28/32 schedule. Our step time is concentrated in the high-resolution group-1 layers (E004/E009 post-mortems), so FLOPs saved at low resolution should turn into wall time better than in a launch-bound net. Our GAP head already works at any resolution. Both shapes must be compiled and warmed up in build (H3.2).

findings.claim: At a fixed 8.5 epochs, the 24 px stage costs -0.124 pp of accuracy with downsampling and -0.188 pp with window-cropping (the difference is 2.8 sigma). Downsampling needs about 0.45 extra epochs to recover that, cropping about 0.8. A 24 px epoch costs 0.575x a 32 px epoch with whole-run CUDA graphs (theory: 0.5625x), but only about 0.82x as charged (about 0.65x steady state) under plain torch.compile. Net effect: -0.081 s with downsampling plus CUDA graph, but +0.03 to +0.10 s (a loss) for the plain-compile, cropping variant. CUDA-graph execution and downsampling each account for about half of the benefit.
findings.relevance: Quantifies the H2.3.1 trade-off and its failure modes. With plain torch.compile, the per-step saving at low resolution is much smaller than FLOPs suggest, so the gain may disappear unless launch overhead is also removed. The predicted >=15% cut is optimistic; about 5-10% is more realistic, and only with downsampling and low overhead.

findings.claim: The whole ~284-step training run was captured as a single CUDA graph, about 5 ms better than per-step graphs. Momentum and weight-decay updates were moved into the compiled graph with torch._foreach_* ops to remove per-step kernel launches. Per-step overhead was about 0.2 ms with the whole-run graph versus 1.5-4 ms with plain torch.compile.
findings.relevance: Suggests a new mechanism the tree lacks. E006 found compile mode barely matters, but compile mode does not address Python and launch overhead from the optimizer (Muon, Lookahead, separate SGD param groups). E007 measured about 4% Muon overhead from small kernels. At 225 steps, 1.5-4 ms/step is about 0.35-0.9 s of our 8.7 s. Proposed hypothesis: capturing the train step plus optimizer step in a CUDA graph (torch.compile mode='reduce-overhead' or manual torch.cuda.graphs, warmed up in build) cuts train time by >=3%.

findings.claim: Hiverge's 94.02% in 1.98 s (vs 2.59 s for airbench94_muon; A100-SXM4-80GB, PyTorch 2.4.0) changes the following. Batch size 1536 (not 2000). Muon lr 0.205, momentum 0.655, 3 NS steps with coefficients (3.4576, -4.7391, 2.0843). Newton-Schulz batched across parameters on padded 3D tensors, with weight renormalization every 4 steps (norm_freq=4) instead of every step. A weight-norm target that anneals from 0.5012 to 0.0786. SGD for bias/norm (lr 0.0573) and head (lr 0.5415) with momentum 0.825. wd 1.04e-6 x batch size. Label smoothing 0.09. GELU replaced by SiLU. Whitening via SVD. Whitening bias trained for 0.2 epochs (was 3). Brightness (0.14) and contrast (0.13) jitter. 7.65 epochs (was 8). Linear LR decay with no warmup. Selective TTA on the 25% least-confident predictions (not allowed here).
findings.relevance: A ready list of Muon tuning ideas for the E007 incumbent (E007 notes 'tune Muon lr/momentum/batch'). Batched Newton-Schulz and less frequent renormalization target the measured ~4% Muon overhead (19.3 vs 18.6 ms per 1000 images). Batch 1536 vs 2000 and SiLU vs GELU are cheap single-variable tests. Hiverge's label smoothing of 0.09 is CIFAR-10 specific, so do not port it over H1.3's 0.3 without a test. Brightness/contrast jitter is an input augmentation, so H1.3 predicts it may hurt in a short schedule; worth a test.

findings.claim: Reference airbench94_muon (94.01% in 2.59 s, n=200): Muon lr 0.24, momentum 0.6, Nesterov, 3 NS steps, batch 2000, 8 epochs, label smoothing 0.2, widths 64/256/256, GELU. BatchNorm uses momentum 0.6, eps 1e-12 and frozen weights (affine weight requires_grad=False). Muon renormalizes each conv weight every step (p.data.mul_(len(p)**0.5 / p.norm())). Whitening bias is trained for the first 3 epochs only. LR decays linearly from the start to 0, with no warmup and no Lookahead. SGD for bias/head (bias_lr 0.053, head_lr 0.67, momentum 0.85), wd 2e-6 x batch size. TTA level 2.
findings.relevance: Check that the E007 Muon port includes per-step weight renormalization and drops Lookahead and the triangular warmup the way airbench94_muon does. Mixing the SGD-era Lookahead and triangular LR with Muon may waste sample efficiency. E007's '~0.24 / 0.6 / batch 2000' matches this script, which was tuned for 64/256/256 widths on CIFAR-10, not 128/384/576 on CIFAR-100, so retuning Muon is plausible.

findings.claim: Several independent agent runs (Opus, GPT) cut the airbench epoch schedule from a padded 10.5 epochs to 9.0-9.75 epochs. That schedule tuning gave 'the large majority of their ~23% improvements'. Specification-gaming examples flagged as illegitimate: precomputing augmentation outside the timed region (~150 ms), selecting faster Modal hosts, and an untimed 60 s GPU cool-down (~9 ms).
findings.relevance: Supports H1: tuning the epoch count and schedule is the main lever, consistent with our ~1 pp/epoch slope. The gaming list warns against moving augmentation into build or the untimed region. RULES require data work in prepare/train, and no sleeps or cool-downs.

findings.claim: airbench96_faster (96.00% in 27.3 s, 3.1 PFLOPs vs airbench96 at 34.7 s, 4.9 PFLOPs) filters data by first training a small proxy model. Per batch of 1024 it keeps the 512 highest-loss examples (mask[loss.argsort()[-512:]] = True), and the masks are reused in the full-size run. The proxy run is extra cost counted in the time. The technique is only shown in the long (~96%) regime.
findings.relevance: Weak or negative evidence for H1.6 as stated. The working variant needs a separate proxy run, not free losses from the current run, and keeps 50% (hard examples). There is no evidence it helps in a ~9-epoch under-trained regime, where every sample still carries signal (our slope is ~1 pp/epoch). With the proxy timed here, a net gain is doubtful; lower H1.6's confidence or test only a cheap in-run variant (losses from the forward pass, skipping the backward pass on easy examples in the last epochs).

findings.claim: Turbo-Muon: an almost-orthogonal preconditioner cuts the starting polar error so one Newton-Schulz iteration can be dropped. It claims ~3% lower training time on several fast-training benchmarks with no hyperparameter tuning, as a drop-in replacement. Drop-Muon updates only a random subset of layers each step and claims the same accuracy up to 1.4x faster in wall-clock time on controlled CNN experiments (datasets not stated in the abstract).
findings.relevance: Optional ways to cut Muon overhead. Our NS already runs 3 steps (airbench default), so Turbo-Muon's gain would likely be <1% here. Drop-Muon's 1.4x is unverified on airbench-style nets and probably comes from reduced backward work on frozen layers. Lower priority than batched Newton-Schulz plus CUDA graphs.

findings.claim: The search snippet says the recipe reached 75.29% in 8.11 s on an A100-SXM4-80GB with an airbench net (128/384/576, label smoothing 0.3, lr 9.0, wd 0.012, 8.5 epochs), and that 'Muon lost to SGD at every size'. The PR page is no longer reachable, so the eval details (TTA or not) cannot be checked.
findings.relevance: E001 measured 73.83% for the same config without TTA, and E007 found Muon beats SGD. The PR's numbers likely include airbench's default TTA, or a different benchmark version (one snippet mentions L40S judging with 50 trials). Treat this source as unreliable and lower the weight of evidence for H1.1/H1.4 that cites it.

findings.claim: The competition repo lists only the organizer's ResNet9 baseline (40 epochs, width 64: 75.36% mean, trials 75.56/75.16, 59.30 s prepare+train, A100 80GB PCIe, 2-trial pilot). It has no pull requests, open or closed, so no competing CIFAR-100 recipes are public.
findings.relevance: No public CIFAR-100-specific record to copy; CIFAR-10 airbench descendants are the best outside source. Our current 8.71 s is about 6.8x faster than the baseline.
